Although it must be admitted that the meaning of language is 
factual question, the general rule is that interpretation 
of a document _a 
a question of law rather than of fact. 4 Williston on Contracts, 3rd Eis 
§ 616. If an issue of contract interpretation 
concerns the intention ~f 
parties, that intention may be determined from the written contract, as 
a matter oflaw, when the nature of the transaction lends itself to judicial 
interpretation. A number of courts, with whom we agree, have recognized 
that contracts between small subcontractors and general contractors on 
large construction projects are such transaction~. (;f, Thos. J. Dyer Co. v. 
Bishop International Engineering Co., 6 Cir., 303 F.2d 655 (1965). The 
reason is that the relationship between the partie,, is a common one and 
usually their intent will not differ from tran action to transaction, 
although it may be differently expressed. 
That intent in most cases is that paym nt by the owner to the 
general contractor is not a condition precedent to the general contractor's 
duty to pay the subcontractors. This is becau. t: • mall subcontractors, who 
must have payment for their work in order to remain in business, will 
not ordinarily assume the risk of the owner's failure to pay the general 
contractor. And this is the reason for the majorit, view in this country, 
which we now join. 
Our decision to require 
judicial int rprc tation of ambiguous 
provisions for final payment in subcontracts in favor of subcontractors 
should not be regarded 
as anti-general c ntnctor. 
It is simply a 
recognition that this is the fairest way to deal w'th the problem. There is 
nothing in this opinion, however, to prevent parties to these contracts 
from shifting the risk of payment failure 
by the owner to the 
subcontractor. But in order to make such a shift the contract must 
unambiguously 
express 
that 
intention. And the burden of clear 
expression is on the general contractor. 
The decisions of the Second District Court of Appeal to affirm the 
summary 
judgments were correct. We adopt, 
therefore, these two 
decisions as the controlling law in Florida and we overrule Gerrits, to the 
extent it is inconsistent with this opinion.
